results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
To keep your tax records in accordance with the IRS rules, follow the schedule below:

| Type of record | Minimum retention period | Source |
|---------------|---------------------------|--------|
| **Records that support an item of income or deduction on a return** | Keep until the **period of limitations** (the time the IRS can assess additional tax or you can amend the return) expires.  | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Copies of filed tax returns** | Keep **forever** (or at least as long as any related limitation period).  | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Employment‑tax records (e.g., payroll, Forms 941/944, W‑2, 1099)** | Keep for at least **4 years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid – whichever is later. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Records relating to property (assets)** | Keep until the **period of limitations** expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Records that are no longer needed for tax purposes but might be required for other purposes (e.g., insurance or creditors)** | Do **not discard** them until you confirm they aren’t needed for those other purposes. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

**Key points**

* The “period of limitations” for most income‑tax returns is 3 years from the filing date, but can extend to 6 years in certain situations (see Table 3 in the publication).  
* For employment‑tax records, the 4‑year rule applies regardless of whether the employee was paid directly (wages) or indirectly (benefits).  
* Asset‑related records are kept longer because they help calculate depreciation, amortization, depletion, and gain or loss on the sale or disposition of the property.  

These rules are taken directly from the IRS Publication 583 – “Starting a Business and Self‑Employment Tax.”



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You need to keep business records for several practical reasons that are spelled out in the company’s own guidance:

1. **To track and improve the business** – Good records let you see whether the business is doing better, which products are selling, and what changes you need to make (Publishing 583, “Recordkeeping” page 15).  

2. **To prepare accurate financial statements** – Income (profit‑and‑loss) statements and balance sheets, which are based on your records, help you work with banks, creditors, and other stakeholders (Publication 583, “Recordkeeping” page 16).  

3. **To support tax returns** – Your records (receipts, invoices, bank statements, etc.) provide the evidence needed to substantiate the income, expenses, and credits you report on your federal tax return, and they must be kept so the IRS can verify them if it examines your return (Publication 583, “Recordkeeping” page 12).  

4. **To satisfy legal and regulatory requirements** – Certain records must be kept to comply with employment‑tax rules, asset‑depreciation rules, and other statutes (Publication 583, “Recordkeeping” page 12–13; OSHA handbook, “Recordkeeping and Reporting” page 15).  

5. **To facilitate future audits or investigations** – A complete set of records speeds up any audit by allowing you to explain items reported, reduce errors, and avoid penalties (Publication 583, “Recordkeeping” page 16).  

These purposes together explain why you must maintain and organize your business records continually.

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
The documents explain that the accounting method you should use depends primarily on whether you keep inventory and on your business’s size.

| Situation | Recommended method | Source |
|-----------|--------------------|--------|
| **You do not have inventory** (most sole‑proprietors, freelancers, contractors, or service‑based businesses) | **Cash method** – record income when you receive it and expenses when you pay them. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **You have inventory** that must be reported to clearly show your income | **Accrual method** – record income when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands, and use accrual for purchases and sales of inventory. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **You are a small‑business taxpayer (average annual gross receipts ≤ $31 million for the prior three years) and have inventory but do not want to keep a full inventory schedule** | **Cash method for all other items, but treat inventory as non‑incidental materials or supplies** – you may still use the cash method overall while accounting for inventory in a way that clearly shows income. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **You have inventory and you choose to keep a traditional inventory ledger** | **Accrual method** and value inventory at the beginning and end of each tax year to calculate cost of goods sold. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |

**How to decide:**
1. **Does your business sell or produce goods that are held for sale?**  
   *If yes → consider inventory requirements (see “Inventories” in the same document).*

2. **Are you a small‑business taxpayer** (average annual receipts ≤ $31 million, not a tax shelter)?  
   *If yes, you may be allowed the special cash‑method treatment for inventory, but you still must use a method that “clearly shows your income.”*

3. **Do you prefer simpler bookkeeping and you have no inventory?**  
   *Cash method is easier and is the default for many sole proprietors.*

**If you later want to change your accounting method** (e.g., from cash to accrual or vice‑versa), you must generally obtain IRS approval, typically by filing **Form 3115, Application for Change in Accounting Method**. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=45) |

So, **use the cash method if you have no inventory and you are a small‑business taxpayer; use the accrual method if you have inventory or if you need to match income and expenses more closely.**



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)
3. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 45)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=45)

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
**How to check your workplace for hazards**

1. **Use the OSHA Small Business Safety & Health Handbook’s “Workplace Self‑Inspection” section** – it explains that the only way to know if hazards exist and whether they are under control is to assess work processes directly (“An effective way to identify workplace hazards is for knowledgeable and experienced workers to conduct routine safety and health inspections (i.e., self‑inspections). The only way to know if potential hazards exist and if they are under control is to assess work processes directly.”) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Follow the handbook’s self‑inspection checklist** –  
   * Identify hazards  
   * Control identified hazards  
   * Monitor and evaluate hazard controls to verify that they continue to be effective [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

   The checklists are intended for general‑industry workplaces, are a starting point, and can be adapted by adding or deleting items to fit your specific processes [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).

3. **Compile the information you gather** – combine completed checklists with injury/illness records, worker training data, and process/equipment logs (maintenance, incident reports). This helps you determine where challenges exist and find solutions [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).

4. **Review OSHA standards and other resources** – the handbook provides links to additional resources on each topic at the end of each checklist [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).

These steps – performing routine self‑inspections using the handbook’s checklists, compiling data, and consulting OSHA standards – are the documented method for checking your workplace for hazards.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 8)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
Cash‑method accounting records income and expenses in the year they are actually received or paid, whereas accrual‑method accounting records income in the year it is earned and expenses in the year they are incurred, even if the cash changes hands in another year.  

**Cash method**  
– “Under the cash method, you report income in the tax year you receive it. You usually deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you pay them” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  
– “Under the cash method, you generally deduct expenses in the tax year in which you actually pay them” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  

**Accrual method**  
– “Under an accrual method of accounting, you generally report income in the year earned and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year incurred” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  
– “Under an accrual method, you generally include an amount in your gross income for the tax year in which all events that fix your right to receive the income have occurred… and you can determine the amount with reasonable accuracy” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  

So, with cash accounting you match income and expenses to the actual cash flow date; with accrual accounting you match them to the time the economic transaction occurs.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)
3. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes.  The Small‑Business Tax Guide says that ordinary and necessary **travel expenses** for a business trip are deductible on Schedule C (Form 1040).  A “business trip” is defined as traveling away from your tax‑home **for a significant period of time** and **requiring sleep or rest** so you can perform your duties (Pub. 334, p. 41).

Typical deductible items for an overnight business trip include:

| Expense | Deductibility (according to the guide) | Notes |
|---------|----------------------------------------|-------|
| **Transportation** (airfare, train, bus, or car) | 100 % of the cost between your home and the business destination | “Travel by airplane, train, bus, or car” is expressly listed (Pub. 334, p. 41). |
| **Taxi, commuter bus, limousine** fares | 100 % for travel between airport/terminal and hotel or between hotel and work location | Included in the “Transportation” listing (Pub. 334, p. 41). |
| **Baggage and shipping** | 100 % | “Cost of sending baggage and sample or display material” (Pub. 334, p. 41). |
| **Car or truck expenses** | 100 % if you use the **actual‑expense method**, or the standard mileage rate (70 ¢/mile for 2025) if you elect that method (Pub. 334, p. 41‑42). |
| **Business‑related tolls and parking** | 100 % | Same rules as car expenses (Pub. 334, p. 42). |
| **Meals** | 50 % of the cost, unless you use the standard meal allowance with Pub. 463 (Pub. 334, p. 41). |
| **Cleaning** (dry‑cleaning, laundry) | 100 % | “Costs of dry cleaning and laundry while on your business trip” (Pub. 334, p. 41). |
| **Telephone** (business calls, fax, other communications) | 100 % | Listed among deductible trip expenses (Pub. 334, p. 41). |
| **Tips** | 100 % | If paid for any of the above services (Pub. 334, p. 41). |

You may also fully deduct the amount you reimburse employees for such travel costs, as long as you document whether the reimbursement is made through an accountable or non‑accountable plan (see Pub. 15, cited in the guide).  

In short, the documents confirm that ordinary and necessary travel expenses—transportation, lodging, meals (½), cleaning, communication, tolls, parking, tips, and employee travel reimbursements—are deductible for a business trip that includes staying overnight or a significant period of time away from your tax‑home.

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
An executive summary is the brief, stand‑alone section that tells the reader the key points of your business plan. According to the SBA Business Planning Guide, it should contain:

* A short, one‑ or two‑paragraph overview of what you want to accomplish.  
* A concise description of the business idea, the amount of money needed, and how that money will be used.  
* A brief outline of the schedule of your major goals and milestones.  

The guide notes that the executive summary is written last because it pulls together information that will appear in the rest of the plan. It is meant to give a reader an immediate snapshot of what the business intends to do and how it plans to get there [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
To describe your target market you should follow the structure outlined in the SBA Business Planning Guide. The guide recommends:

1. **Define the market niche**  
   * Identify who your best customer is.  
   * Describe that customer’s characteristics.  
   (SBA Business Planning Guide, page 14)  

2. **Segment the market**  
   * For **business markets**: classify by industry, company size, location, or product use/application.  
   * For **consumer (household) markets**: segment by demographics (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application, or benefits sought.  
   (SBA Business Planning Guide, page 14)  

3. **Estimate size and growth**  
   * Approximate the total size of the target market and its growth potential.  
   * Use population figures, sales‑tax data, industry information, etc., to estimate how much of the total market you aim to capture.  
   (SBA Business Planning Guide, page 14)  

4. **Explain why customers will switch**  
   * Discuss what will make customers leave competitors and choose your business.  
   * Highlight features you offer that competitors can’t easily copy and how you will counter competitive reactions.  
   (SBA Business Planning Guide, page 15)  

These points give a clear, structured way to articulate who your target market is and why they will choose you.

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes, if your shop is open to the public you are required to provide a **wheelchair‑accessible entrance, route, and key service areas**. The ADA guide for small businesses states:

* **Enabling entrance:** If a business has two public entrances, at least one must be accessible. If only one entrance exists, that entrance must be accessible. When one entrance is not accessible, you must provide a second accessible entrance or a shortcut (ramp, lift, etc.) and sign any alternative entrance with a direction to it. The alternative entrance must be open during store hours, and any door-hardware that requires tight grasping is not compliant. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)

* **Accessible route:** The path from the sidewalk or parking to the accessible entrance must have no steps or steeply‑sloped surfaces and must be firm, stable, and slip‑resistant. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)

* **Accessible sales/service counter (if you sell goods or services):** At least one counter or a lowered section of a counter must be no higher than 36 inches above the floor and at least 36 inches long, with a clear space of 30 inches × 48 inches in front of it for a wheelchair. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

* **Door hardware:** All main doors should be at least 36 inches wide and must use lever‑type handles or other grasp‑free hardware. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)

* **Parking (if you provide parking):** For every 25–50 spaces, you must provide an accessible parking space, which must include a 5‑ft‑wide access aisle (for cars) or an 8‑ft wide aisle (for vans) and a clearly marked sign. The accessible parking must be on a level path that leads to the accessible entrance. (ada_guide_small_business.pdf, pages 8‑9)

In short, a small shop that is open to customers must:  
1. Make at least one entrance wheelchair‑safe and provide an accessible route to it;  
2. Sign and keep open any alternative entrance;  
3. Equip a sales or service counter in an accessible manner;  
4. Use compliant door hardware; and  
5. Provide accessible parking if you offer any parking.  

If any of these points are not feasible, the guide suggests considering alternative arrangements—such as staff assistance or a secondary accessible location—but “doing so must be readily achievable.” (ada_guide_small_business.pdf, pages 15‑16)



**Sources:**
1. [ada_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 10)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)
2. [ada_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

results.question: how many employees before ada employment rules apply
results.answer:

results.question: how long do i have to report a workplace death
results.answer:
All work‑related fatalities must be reported to OSHA **within 8 hours** of the incident. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

results.question: when do i report an amputation to osha
results.answer: Amputations must be reported to OSHA within **24 hours** of the incident (or the occurrence of the injury) — the same time frame that OSHA requires for all work‑related fatalities, inpatient hospitalizations, and loss of an eye. ( OSHA Small Business Safety and Health Handbook, page 15 )

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
Based on the company’s OSHA Handbook, you are **partially exempt from the standard injury‑recordkeeping requirements only if**

* **Your business had 10 or fewer workers during every month of the last calendar year** (or *or* you are in one of the “low‑hazard” industries listed in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A). ( **osha_small_business_handbook.pdf, page 14** )  
* Even when exempt from completing Form 300 (the Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses log), **you still must report** any work‑related **fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye** to OSHA, and you do not waive those reporting obligations. ( **osha_small_business_handbook.pdf, page 14** )

If you exceed 10 employees or are not in a low‑hazard industry, you must keep and maintain the full OSHA injury recordkeeping system (Forms 300, 301, 300A, and any required electronic submissions). ( **osha_small_business_handbook.pdf, page 15** )

results.question: how long do i keep injury records
results.answer: In an OSHA‑covered workplace you must keep all injury and illness records (OSHA Form 300, Form 301, and Form 300A) on site for **at least five years** (the 5‑year retention period applies even if your business is exempt from the broader OSHA record‑keeping requirement).

results.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
results.answer:
**Tax‑related records**

| What to keep | How long to keep |
|--------------|------------------|
| 1. **All records that support an item of income or an item of deduction on a tax return** – e.g., invoices, receipts, deposit slips, canceled checks, payroll records, business‑checkbook entries, etc. | Keep them for **the period of limitations** for that return – the time in which you could amend the return or the IRS could assess additional tax. (See IRS Pub. 583, “How Long To Keep Records,” p. 16) |
| 2. **Copies of filed tax returns** | Keep them **forever** (they assist with future returns and amended returns). (IRS Pub. 583, p. 16) |
| 3. **Employment‑tax records** (e.g., Forms 941/944, payroll tax deposits, payroll‑related W‑2s, etc.) | Keep all employment‑tax records for **at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**. (IRS Pub. 583, p. 16) |
| 4. **Asset‑related records** – purchase price, improvements, depreciation, sale documents, etc. | Keep them **until the period of limitations expires for the year in which the asset is disposed of in a taxable disposition**. (IRS Pub. 583, p. 16) |
| 5. **Other records that may be required by insurers or creditors** | Retain longer than the IRS requires if those parties demand it. (IRS Pub. 583, p. 16) |

**Injury/Illness record‑keeping (OSHA)**  

| What to keep | How long to keep | When to file/notify |
|--------------|------------------|---------------------|
| 1. **Log all occupational injuries and illnesses** that are not minor first‑aid incidents on **OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)**. | Keep **at the worksite for at least 5 years**. (OSHA Small‑Business Handbook, p. 15) |
| 2. **Injury/illness incident report** for each recordable case on **OSHA Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report)** (or an equivalent form that supplies the same information). | Same 5‑year retention as Form 300. (OSHA Small‑Business Handbook, p. 15) |
| 3. **Annual summary** of the year's injuries/illnesses on **OSHA Form 300A (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)**. | Same 5‑year retention as the log/incident reports. (OSHA Small‑Business Handbook, p. 15) |
| 4. **Electronic submission** of Forms 300 (log) and 301 (incident reports) for certain establishments (250+ workers or 20–249 workers in specific high‑hazard industries). | Submit the summary **by March 2 of the year after the calendar year covered** by the form. (OSHA Small‑Business Handbook, p. 14–15) |
| 5. **Fatalities** | Report **within 8 hours** of the event. (OSHA Small‑Business Handbook, p. 15) |
| 6. **In‑patient hospitalizations, amputations and loss of an eye** | Report **within 24 hours** of the event. (OSHA Small‑Business Handbook, p. 15) |

The OSHA handbook also indicates that work‑related fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations and eye‑loss cases must be reported to OSHA regardless of the establishment’s size or industry (OSHA Small‑Business Handbook, p. 14).

---

**Summary**  
- **Tax records:** keep all documents that support your tax filings until the IRS period‑of‑limitations period (usually the later of 3–6 years, depending on the type of item). Keep employment‑tax records for at least 4 years, asset records until the end of the disposal year’s limitations period, and keep copies of all filed returns permanently.  
- **Injury records:** keep OSHA Forms 300, 301, and 300A on site for at least 5 years, file the annual 300A summary electronically by March 2 (if required), and report fatalities within 8 hours and severe injuries within 24 hours.

results.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
results.answer:
**How to start a business and keep your taxes organized**

| Step | What you need to do | Key document(s) & page(s) |
|------|---------------------|---------------------------|
| **1. Decide on a legal structure** | Choose whether you’ll operate as a sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, or limited‑liability company (LLC). The choice affects tax forms, liability, and reporting. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 10 (“Determining Which Type of Business to Use”) |
| **2. Get a taxpayer identification number (TIN)** | If you’ll hire employees or pay excise tax, obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN). Even sole proprietors without employees can get an EIN to keep business and personal id numbers separate. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 12 (“IRS Employer Tax ID Number”) |
| **3. File any required state registrations** | Check whether you need to file a fictitious name (assumed business name), articles of incorporation, or articles of organization with the Secretary of State. | sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 6 (“Legal Structure for Your Business”) |
| **4. Set up a separate business bank account** | Keep business funds separate from personal funds. Use the business checkbook to record all income and expenses. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 14 (“Business checkbook”) |
| **5. Pick a bookkeeping method** | For a small business, a single‑entry or double‑entry system can be used. Record transactions daily; keep journals and ledgers if using double‑entry. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 15 (“Bookkeeping System”) |
| **6. Keep records of all transactions** | For each sale, purchase, payroll, or other transaction, keep supporting documents (sales slips, receipts, deposit slips, canceled checks, invoices). | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 12 (“Supporting Documents”) |
| **7. Store records electronically or in hard copy** | Either format must preserve the content, allow retrieval, and be available for IRS inspection. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 12 (“Electronic records”) |
| **8. Follow the required retention period** | Keep records supporting income or deductions until the applicable tax‑limitations period ends (typically 3–6 years, longer for employment taxes). | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 16 (“How Long To Keep Records”) |
| **9. File the appropriate tax returns each year** | Sole proprietors use Schedule C (Form 1040). Corporations use Form 1120, LLCs use Form 1065, etc. File by the deadlines indicated for each tax year. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 11 (“Business Income”) |
| **10. Deduct eligible business expenses** | Only ordinary and necessary expenses can be deducted. Keep receipts and documentation to prove each deduction. | irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 32 (“Business Expenses”) |
| **11. Reconcile your bank statements monthly** | Compare your checkbook and books with bank statements to catch errors early. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 14 (“Reconciling the checking account”) |
| **12. Stay compliant with employment taxes if you hire** | Keep employment‑tax records for at least 4 years after the tax becomes due. | irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 16 (“Employment taxes”) |

**Why these steps keep your taxes organized**

* **Separate records** – A dedicated business bank account, separate checkbook, and clear source labels prevent mixing personal and business funds, simplifying both accounting and tax reporting.  
* **Consistent record‑keeping** – Daily recording of receipts and expenses ensures you have supporting documentation for every deduction and income item, meeting IRS evidence requirements.  
* **Retention schedule** – Following the IRS‑specified periods guarantees you have the paperwork if the agency later questions any return, reducing the risk of penalties.  
* **Regular reconciliation** – Monthly bank‑statement checks catch counting or entry errors early, preventing bigger discrepancies when you prepare tax returns.  

By following the steps above, using the documents listed for detailed guidance, you’ll have a clear path to launch your business and maintain organized, compliant tax records.

results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
To keep workers safe and to make your premises accessible, the company document set requires you to:

1. **Establish a Safety‑and‑Health Program**  
   - Create a program that covers **management leadership, worker participation, hazard identification and assessment, hazard prevention and control, education and training, program evaluation and improvement, and communication & coordination for host employers, contractors, and staffing agencies**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)  
   - Conduct regular workplace inspections to spot hazards and fix them immediately [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7).  
   - Use OSHA’s tools, such as the safety‑and‑health program checklist and self‑evaluation tool, to guide implementation [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7).  

2. **Meet the General Duty Clause**  
   - Provide a work environment “free from recognized hazards that are causing or are likely to cause death or serious physical harm” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91).  

3. **Ensure Physical Accessibility (ADA)**  
   - **Entrances** – A single step can block entry for people using wheelchairs; use an alternate accessible entrance or a ramp with an edge‑protective handrail. The ramp slope should be no steeper than 1:12, and handrails are required if the slope is greater than 1:20 and the rise exceeds 6 in. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  
   - **Parking** – Provide accessible parking spaces that are close to an accessible entrance and have a 5‑foot‑wide access aisle. The number of spaces depends on the total parking capacity: 1 space for ≤25 cars, 2 spaces for ≤50 cars, etc. (ada_guide_small_business.pdf, pages 9‑11).  
   - **Signage** – Place an international symbol of accessibility on accessible entrances, parking spaces, and alternate doors, mounted at a height not higher than 48 in. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  
   - **Interior Circulation** – All internal routes that connect accessible entrances to other parts of the building must be free of steps and steep slopes, have a firm, slip‑resistant surface, and allow a clear 36‑in‑wide path for wheelchairs [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  

4. **Accessible Services (e.g., counters, tables)**  
   - Sales and service counters should have a 36‑in‑long, no higher than 36‑in. pickup surface and provide a 30 × 48 in. clear space in front. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)  
   - For fixed tables, at least 5 % (or one if fewer than 20 tables) must be accessible, with a table height of 28–34 in., knee clearance of at least 27 in., and a clear 30 × 48 in. area in front. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17)  

5. **Ongoing Evaluation & Improvement**  
   - Use OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation Program to have experts review your safety and health program, identify gaps, and help you improve [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90).  

By tying together the OSHA‑mandated safety‑and‑health program and the ADA‑mandated accessibility requirements, you’ll protect employees from workplace hazards and ensure that all visitors—regardless of disability—can safely access your premises.

**What to keep track of for taxes**

**Record‑keeping guidelines**

By tracking each of these items in the manner described, you will have the documentation required to calculate and support all deductible tax and travel expenses on your federal tax return.

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
**Do you need an EIN?**  
Yes, if you meet any of the following conditions you must obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN):  

* You pay wages to one or more employees.  
* You file pension or excise tax returns.  
(Otherwise a sole‑propeller can use their Social‑Security number.) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

**What accounting method “comes with” an EIN?**  
An EIN does **not** lock your business into a particular accounting method.  
When you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040), you choose an accounting method (cash, accrual, special, or combination) and must use that method consistently. The choice of EIN has no effect on which accounting method you select. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=45)



**Sources:**

2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 45)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=45)

results.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
results.answer:
For injury and illness record‑keeping you must keep the following OSHA forms:

* OSHA **Form 300** – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses  
* OSHA **Form 301** – Injury and Illness Incident Report (a supplementary record for each case)  
* OSHA **Form 300A** – Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses (prepared annually)  

These forms must be retained at the worksite for **at least five years** (the period required for OSHA’s 300, 301, and 300A records) .

results.question: how do i register a trademark
results.answer:
To register a trademark you’ll need to work through either your state’s trademark office or the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) for federal registration.

1. **Check that the mark isn’t already taken** – search the state and/or federal trademark databases before filing.  
2. **File the application** – you can file at the state level (e.g., South Dakota Secretary of State) or the federal level (USPTO).  
3. **Contact the appropriate office for guidance** –  
   * South Dakota Secretary of State: (605) 773‑2797, https://sdsos.gov/  
   * U.S. Patent and Trademark Office: (703) 308‑HELP or (800) 786‑9199, www.uspto.gov [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)
